newsitem.title: UK: Britain condemns nationalist violence in N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Britain condemns nationalist violence in N.Ireland.

text.p: Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, on Monday condemned "orchestrated violence" that swept through Irish nationalist communities in the province overnight in protest at a Protestant parade.
Despite appeals for calm, Catholic youths continued to hijack cars and set them ablaze in protest at the routing of a Protestant parade down the Catholic zone of rural Portadown.

Catholic Irish nationalists led by senior Sinn Fein leader Martin McGuinness clashed briefly with police guarding a Protestant march in Bellaghy, 40 miles (60 km) northwest of Belfast, but no serious incidents were reported.
The march, one of dozens being staged at the climax of the Protestant "marching season", was being staged in a staunchly Catholic area but had been rerouted because of Catholic opposition.
McGuinness, whose party is the political wing of Catholic-backed Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas, was struck on the head in the scuffles but was not badly hurt.

Emergency service sirens wailed around Belfast as police rushed to several incidents in which cars were hijacked and set on fire, but the violence was minor compared to the fury that greeted Sunday's Protestant Orange Order parade in Portadown.
Police investigated the death of a Protestant youth found near the site of a small explosion in south Belfast. They refused to confirm or deny that he was handling a bomb.

Sunday marked Northern Ireland's worst outbreak of nationalist unrest in years as rioters and police clashed in Belfast, Londonderry and other towns after an Orange Order march through a Catholic area of Portadown.
Two 14-year-old boys were badly hurt -- one by gunfire and one by a plastic bullet fired as a riot control measure by the beleaguered Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) police.
Three police officers had narrow escapes -- one was hit by a bullet to the helmet, a bullet hit another on the lapel microphone he was using and a third was saved by a flak jacket.
Police said more than 80 people had been injured in the past 36 hours. More than 1,600 plastic bullets were fired, there were 500 attacks on security forces and 691 petrol bombs were thrown.

Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams, whose party sees itself as the voice of radical Irish nationalism, called on youths to end car hijackings and the burning of property. The party wants an end to British rule of Northern Ireland.
Adams was seen trying to end the hijacking of a lorry in Catholic West Belfast to return the vehicle to its owner.
Mowlam told a Belfast news conference: "I understand the anger in nationalist communities, but nothing justified the orchestrated violence that we have seen in the last 24 hours."
British Prime Minister Tony Blair backed Mowlam and pledged to press on with the search for peace through year-old talks.
"We are going to go on searching for peace," Blair told reporters. "We will not give up, even for a moment."
Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern, whose government is co-sponsor with London of the fragile peace process, held more talks with Blair on Monday.

"Like any violence it has to be condemned. The frustrations of nationalist people are I think understood but I would just far prefer to see all these matters dealt with and handled in a peaceful way," Ahern told reporters.
Mowlam called on the Orange Order to display "willingness and understanding" as their annual "marching season" reaches its high point this week.
"There can and should be no triumphalism," she said.
The IRA and breakaway Irish National Liberation Army fired dozens of bullets overnight and appeared to signal the end of any honeymoon with Britain's new Labour government.

"The events that we saw over the past 24 hours were provoked by the shameful decision of the British government to capitulate to the Orange Order's demands to march through nationalist areas where there is fear and trepidation at their presence," Sinn Fein chairman Mitchel McLaughlin said.
David Trimble, leader of the pro-British Ulster Unionist Party, said the IRA had been planning violence.
"I think that came out very clearly last night, with the clearly prepared reaction that the IRA orchestrated throughout Northern Ireland.
